list.listitem: The history and physical examination are not very accurate for differentiating the causes of dyspepsia. C

Patients over the age of 60 years with new onset dyspepsia and patients at increased risk for malignancy due to residency in a high-risk country for gastric cancer or family history should be referred for prompt upper endoscopy. B
Patients under age 60 years should be tested for Helicobacter pylori (HP) and treated accordingly.B

If the test and treat strategy is chosen, test for HP with either the C13 urea breath test (preferred) or stool antigen test; patients should not take a PPI or antibiotics for 2 weeks prior to testing. B

If HP eradication is unsuccessful or if HP negative, proceed to a trial of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), tricyclic antidepressant (TCA), or prokinetic agent; if those are not successful, consider endoscopy. B
Patients with normal endoscopy and persistent epigastric pain have functional dyspepsia and should undergo HP eradication and, in turn, trials of PPI, TCA, prokinetic, or psychotherapy. B

background.definition: Dyspepsia describes a set of symptoms including pain, discomfort or burning in the upper abdomen. Bloating, belching, early satiety, nausea, and vomiting are also associated symptoms in some people. The Rome IV diagnostic criteria for functional dyspepsia are the presence of at least one of the following symptoms for at least 3 months (bothersome postprandial fullness, early satiation, epigastric pain, and/or epigastric burning) AND no evidence of structural disease (including at upper endoscopy) that is likely to explain the symptoms.

list.listitem: Three-month incidence: 8 to 10 per 1000 adults.
New-onset dyspepsia occurs in 2.8% of adults per year, based on a population H. pylori screening study.
Fourteen percent of adults in the United States.

Global prevalence of uninvestigated dyspepsia based on Rome III criteria is 5% to 11% but increases to 29.5% when a broad definition is used. In this study, prevalence was higher among women, smokers, users of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and individuals who were H. pylori-positive.
In a systematic review, prevalence of dyspepsia was 27%.

Authors of a more recent systematic review found a pooled US prevalence of dyspeptic symptoms of 16.3% (95% confidence interval [CI], 9.1%-25.1%). Combined prevalence of dyspeptic and/or gastroesophageal symptoms was 35.2% (95% CI, 14.9%-58.9%).
Functional dyspepsia rates in children range from 3.5% to 27%.
Patients with dyspepsia have higher medical costs of $3580 per year and 14 more visits per year.
Patients with functional dyspepsia versus those without also have higher medical costs of $5138 per year and greater work absenteeism (0.83 absence days/year).
In a systematic review, the prevalence of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in subjects with dyspepsia was 37% compared with 7% in those without dyspepsia (OR 8; 95% CI, 5.74-11.16).

IBS and functional dyspepsia are also associated with atopy, making activation of the immune system a possible contributing factor. This link is only partly explained by a common connection with mood disorders.
Authors of a meta-analysis found a pooled prevalence of dyspepsia of 65.7% (95% CI, 51-79%) in patients with cholecystolithiasis, although there was large heterogeneity across studies.
In another systematic review of patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), dyspeptic symptoms were present in 38% (range, 21%-63%).
With respect to work productivity, among active workers in Brazil with dyspepsia, 32.2% reported that dyspepsia had caused work absenteeism and 78% reported a reduction in work productivity.
There is a positive association between functional dyspepsia and depression with an OR of 2.28 (95% CI, 2.02-3.81) based on a meta-analysis of 23 studies with 59,029 subjects.
Effect of gastrin and stomach acid on gastroduodenal mucosa, leading to inflammation or ulceration or abnormal duodenal sensitivity to acid.

Delayed gastric emptying: more than one in four patients with functional dyspepsia have evidence of delayed gastric emptying and there is considerable overlap in the pathophysiological features of gastroparesis and functional dyspepsia.
Direct irritation by medications, alcohol, tobacco.
Discontinuation of a PPI.
Infection with H. pylori.
Post-infectious (may be part of a larger grouping of hyperesthesia or abnormal gastric sensation).
Rarely, malignancy or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Differential.Differential_Features: Absence of structural pathology; reserved for patients with a negative upper endoscopy
Night-time awakening with pain; presence of ulcer on upper endoscopy
Repeated episodes of reflux and heartburn: good predictors of GERD
Difficult to distinguish from functional dyspepsia; early satiety, weight loss, delayed gastric emptying (breath test or scintigraphy)
Intermittent episodes of right upper quadrant pain usually following meals
Travel history, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, fatigue, positive stool for ova and parasites
Symptoms can include chest pain or pressure, sweating, shortness of breath, nausea or vomiting. History of heart disease
Dyspepsia associated with medication use, eg, NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, antibiotics, corticosteriods
Pain in back, elevated lipase, and amylase
Epigastric pain, diarrhea, elevated serum gastrin levels, and abnormal secretin stimulation test

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: Using Rome IV criteria, adult patients are diagnosed with functional dyspepsia if they have one or more of: bothersome postprandial fullness, early satiation, epigastric pain and/or burning with no structural disease (including on endoscopy) to explain the symptoms. For a child/adolescent, Rome IV removed the dictum "no evidence for organic disease" in all definitions and replaced it with "after appropriate medical evaluation the symptoms cannot be attributed to another medical condition". See chapter on non-ulcer dyspepsia.

list.listitem: British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidelines recommend urgent evaluation of patients with UGI alarm symptoms, such as anyone with dysphagia, or persons 55 years or older with weight loss and either dyspepsia, upper abdominal pain, or reflux. They also recommend urgent evaluation for patients 40 years or older who are either from a region where gastric cancer is common or who have a family history of gastroesophageal cancer. Other alarm symptoms warranting a less urgent evaluation include hematemesis; and in persons 55 years or older, treatment-resistant dyspepsia, dyspepsia, or upper abdominal pain with elevated platelet count, low hemoglobin, nausea or vomiting, or nausea or vomiting with any weight loss, reflux, dyspepsia, or upper abdominal pain.

In general, the history and physical examination are not very accurate in differentiating the causes of dyspepsia and there is a high degree of symptom overlap between gastroesophageal reflux disease, functional dyspepsia, IBS. Food relieving pain, nighttime awakening with pain, and episodic pain best predict ulcer.
Being over the ages of 45 years (primarily in areas where gastric cancer is common) or 55 years and the presence of alarm signs and symptoms increase the risk of malignancy (see ).
The age cutoff varies with different guidelines; there is some evidence that the age cutoff should be lower for men than for women, but this is not part of current guidelines.

In one large Chinese study, among over 15,000 patients with alarm symptoms, 14.8% had an upper GI malignancy; only dysphagia among patients between the ages of 36 years and 74 years had a positive likelihood ratio >10 for malignancy. In an Iranian study of 2,847 patients with dyspepsia, 66.7% of patients with cancer had at least one alarm symptoms vs. 38.9% of patients without cancer. Although single alarm symptoms were poor predictors, a combination of age, alarm symptoms, and smoking distinguished between high and low-risk patients with an area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of 0.85.

Medications, eg, NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, calcium antagonists, nitrates, theophylline, antibiotics, and corticosteroids can be an important cause of dyspepsia. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends reviewing medications for possible causes of dyspepsia and, in those needing referral, suspending NSAID use.
Other signs that should prompt immediate evaluation are the presence of jaundice or abdominal mass.
In general, physical examination is not useful since most patients will have only epigastric tenderness.

Using a cutoff of 3% risk (from NICE), dysphagia or changes in bowel habits in men and rectal bleeding in women should trigger referral for further workup to exclude cancer or IBD. In addition, abdominal pain, changes in bowel habits, or dyspepsia in patients older than 60 years should be investigated since they predict cancer or IBD in more than 3% of both men and women.
A systematic review found that about 5% of patients with dyspepsia are eventually diagnosed with celiac disease.
BSG guidelines recommend against the routine use of gastric emptying tests or 24-hour pH monitoring.

As part of the initial evaluation, BSG guidelines recommend that all patients 55 years or older should have a complete blood count with platelets, those with overlapping irritable bowel symptoms should have celiac serology, and those 60 years or older with abdominal pain and weight loss should have an abdominal CT to evaluate for pancreatic cancer.

BSG guidelines recommend that all patients with dyspepsia should be evaluated for the presence of HP using a stool or breath test and, if the results are abnormal, the patient should be treated to eradicate HP (another recent study confirms that eradication not only reduces the risk of ulcer but is also effective for functional dyspepsia). Confirmation of HP eradication is only recommended for patients at increased risk of gastric cancer, although it should also be considered in patients whose symptoms persist.

The stool antigen and urea breath tests (using either C13 or C14) are the most accurate test for the presence of H. pylori. Either test is recommended for diagnosis in the most recent Maastricht IV/Florence consensus report.
Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that the C13 urea breath test was the most accurate diagnostic test, and was significantly more accurate than other tests including stool antigen tests.

Proton pump inhibitors, bismuth, and antibiotics can interfere with both tests by reducing bacterial load in the stomach and lead to false-negative results. They should be stopped for at least 2 weeks so as not to interfere with testing. H2-receptor antagonists do not affect bacterial load and can be used when discontinuing a PPI.

Testing for successful eradication following treatment seems reasonable even in asymptomatic patients. The urea breath test or stool antigen test can be used to confirm eradication. NICE guidelines recommend C13 urea breath test for eradication testing.
Among stool antigen tests, the Amplified IDEIA Hp StAR (90% sensitivity, 89% specificity) was significantly more sensitive than ImmunoCard STAT! HpSA and more specific than RAPID Hp StAR.
Serologic testing (both laboratory and in-office) is less accurate.

For patients with dyspepsia and suspected atrophic gastritis (AG), a blood test called GastroPanel® that measures pepsinogen I and II, gastrin-17, and H. pylori antibodies was found to be 82.9% sensitivity for the diagnosis of AG in one small study of 47 patients. As the test does not reflect severity of AG, it is not clear if the results of this test will avoid endoscopy for these patients.

Upper endoscopy is preferred over double-contrast upper GI imaging because of accuracy, ability to perform biopsies, and ability to test directly for H. pylori with a CLOtest Rapid Urease Test. In one study, use of dual specimens (antrum and body) increased sensitivity of rapid urease test and reduced reaction duration to 30 minutes. In another study, both the Pyloritek and 5-min rapid urease test performed better than the CLO test.

Abnormalities on upper endoscopy were shown in one cross-sectional study to be only weakly associated with symptoms. In this study,18% of asymptomatic persons, 25% with dyspepsia but no reflux, 30% with dyspepsia and reflux, 34% with reflux alone, and 35% with alarm symptoms or signs had abnormal endoscopic findings (esophagitis, BE, PUD, erosions, or neoplasia).
Based on a systematic review, 70% of patients with dyspepsia have functional dyspepsia, less than 10% have peptic ulcer disease, and less than 1% have cancer.

Similarly, in a study of 282 Brazilian patients, mean age 44 years, with uninvestigated dyspepsia, functional dyspepsia was found in 66%, while 18% had GERD and 13% had an ulcer. Forty-five percent of the patients reported alarm symptoms and three of the four cases of gastric adenocarcinoma (1.4%) were identified among these patients.

In a meta-analysis of nine studies of endoscopy for patients with dyspepsia, erosive gastritis was the most common abnormality identified (13.4% pooled prevalence) followed by peptic ulcer (8% pooled prevalence); only peptic ulcer was found more frequently in individuals with versus without dyspepsia (OR 2.07; 95% CI, 1.52-2.82).

In a study of 1167 Chinese and Malaysian patients with uninvestigated dyspepsia presenting for endoscopy, about one quarter had clinically significant findings. Independent risk factors for significant findings were H. pylori infection (OR 2.36; 95% CI, 1.83-3.26), male gender (OR 1.84; 95% CI, 1.53-2.59), age 45 years or older (OR 1.82; 95% CI, 1.38-2.48), and duration of dyspepsia for 5 or more months (OR 1.44; 95% CI, 1.13-2.03). Given the difference in healthcare systems, it is not clear whether these findings are similar to those in Europe or North America.

Among consecutive men and women with dyspepsia but without alarm symptoms, malignancy was found in 8 of 3859 men and women under age 45 years (0.21%) and in 30/5049 (0.59%) 45 years and older. Among women, only 2 of 2661 under age 57 years had malignancy, compared with 2 of 1209 among men under age 35 years.
A clinical decision rule based on signs, symptoms and body mass index predicts which patients with dyspepsia are likely to benefit from omeprazole.
A clinical rule is reasonably accurate at predicting the likelihood of ulcer but is impractical for routine use.

A simple 5-item score consisting of age >40 years, albumin ≤3.5 g/dl, hemoglobin ≤11 g/dl, recent onset of symptoms, and the presence of any alarm symptom predicted the risk of malignancy in a population of 2324 Indian patients with dyspepsia undergoing upper endoscopy.

listitem.strong: American College of Gastroenterology / Canadian Academy of Gastroenterology Guidelines (2017)

list.listitem: Previous guidelines recommended that patients with alarm signs and symptoms at any age (see ) should be referred for immediate endoscopy. The most recent ACG/CAG guidelines, though, do not recommend routine endoscopy for alarm symptoms in patients under age 60 years due to their poor predictive value.

ACG/CAG guidelines recommend endoscopy for patients with dyspepsia older than 60 years. Patients younger than 60 years who come from countries at high risk for gastric cancer or who have a family history should also consider endoscopy.

For patients younger than 60 years with dyspepsia, test for H. pylori. If positive, treat for H. pylori. If negative for HP, or symptoms persist following HP eradication, give trials of a PPI, a tricyclic antidepressant, or a prokinetic agent, or consider referral for upper endoscopy. The same general approach is recommended for any patient with functional dyspepsia (dyspepsia symptoms with normal endoscopy).
For patients with GERD predominant symptoms, under age 60 years, and no red flags, a trial of a H2RA or PPI is an option.

NICE guidelines recommend that people presenting with dyspepsia together with significant acute gastrointestinal bleeding be referred immediately (on the same day) to a specialist. They also recommend referral to specialist care for patients of any age with gastroesophageal symptoms who are non responsive to treatment or unexplained, with suspected GERD who are considering surgery, and for those with H. pylori unresponsive to second-line eradication therapy.

Upper gastrointestinal biopsy in the absence of visible lesions may be warranted in adult patients under investigation for dyspepsia with endoscopy who are immunocompromised or when their H. pylori status is unknown.

feature.caption: Alarm Signs and Symptoms in Patients with Dyspepsia.
feature.feature_body:
• Age >45-55 years*
• Iron-deficiency anemia (unexplained)
• Dysphagia or odynophagia
• Gastrointestinal bleeding
• Persistent vomiting
• Involuntary weight loss of at least 5%
• Palpable mass
• Jaundice
• Family history of gastric cancer
*Age cutoff varies in different guidelines. Data from Meineche-Schmidt V, Jørgensen T. "Alarm symptoms" in patients with dyspepsia: a three-year prospective study from general practice. Scand J Gastroenterol 2002:37;999-1007; Graham DY, Rugge M. Clinical practice: diagnosis and evaluation of dyspepsia. J Clin Gastroenterol 2010;44(3):167-172.
